title: Quality Factor (Q-factor) in Alternating Current Circuits
short_intro: The quality factor (Q-factor) is a dimensionless parameter that characterizes the resonance sharpness and energy storage capacity of an underdamped resonant electrical circuit. It represents the ratio of maximum energy stored per cycle to the energy dissipated per radian.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of Q-factor for series L-C-R circuits, dependence on circuit parameters (L, C, R), resonance frequency, and bandwidth relationships.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of Q-factor using potential drop magnification across reactive components at resonance, parallel LCR circuits, and energy-based definitions.

prerequisites: Impedance and phase angle in AC circuits
Power dissipation and RMS values in AC

concept_notes.heading: Physical Definition and Significance
bullets: Q-factor is defined as 2π times the maximum energy stored divided by the energy dissipated per cycle.
It quantifies the sharpness of the resonance curve: a higher Q-factor implies a narrower resonance peak and lower damping.
In a radio receiver or tuner, a high Q-factor ensures high selectivity for a specific frequency.

concept_notes.heading: Q-factor in a Series L-C-R Circuit
bullets: At resonance, inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance (ω<sub>r</sub>L = 1/(ω<sub>r</sub>C)).
The Q-factor equals the ratio of resonant angular frequency to bandwidth (ω<sub>r</sub> / Δω).
It can also be expressed as the ratio of voltage across either inductor or capacitor to the applied source voltage at resonance.

concept_notes.heading: Bandwidth and Selectivity
bullets: Bandwidth (Δω) is defined as the frequency interval between the two half-power points where power drops to half its maximum value.
The relation between bandwidth, resonant frequency, and Q-factor is given by Δω = ω<sub>r</sub> / Q.
Damping resistance R broadens the bandwidth and lowers the Q-factor.

concept_notes.heading: Q-factor in a Parallel L-C-R Circuit
bullets: In a parallel resonant circuit, the Q-factor is given by the ratio of the parallel resistance to the inductive reactance at resonance.
It determines the magnification of circulating current in the parallel branch compared to the total source current.
High parallel resistance yields a high Q-factor and sharper rejection of off-resonance frequencies.

derivations.title: Derivation of Q-factor for Series L-C-R Circuit using Voltage Magnification
derivations.conditions: Series L-C-R circuit operating at angular resonance frequency ω<sub>r</sub>
steps: At resonance, inductive reactance X<sub>L</sub> = ω<sub>r</sub>L and capacitive reactance X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ω<sub>r</sub>C) are equal, and circuit impedance is minimum: Z = R.
The maximum voltage across the inductor at resonance is V<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>max</sub> X<sub>L</sub> = (V<sub>rms</sub> / R) ω<sub>r</sub>L.
The Q-factor is defined as the voltage magnification: Q = V<sub>L</sub> / V<sub>rms</sub> = (ω<sub>r</sub>L) / R.

derivations.title: Derivation of Q-factor from Bandwidth and Resonance Frequency
steps: The half-power frequencies occur where the total impedance Z = R&sqrt;2, making the current drop to I<sub>max</sub> / &sqrt;2.
The difference between the two half-power frequencies defines the bandwidth: Δω = ω<sub>2</sub> - ω<sub>1</sub>.
Solving the resonant circuit equations yields the half-power bandwidth as Δω = R / L.
Substituting ω<sub>r</sub> = 1 / &sqrt;LC and Δω = R / L gives the ratio Q = ω<sub>r</sub> / Δω.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Frequency Response Curve (Current vs Frequency) for Different Q-factors
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of rms current (I<sub>rms</sub>) on the y-axis versus frequency (f) on the x-axis, showing multiple resonance peaks for different values of resistance R (high R gives a broad, flat peak; low R gives a sharp, high peak).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Lower resistance R leads to a higher Q-factor, resulting in a sharper resonance peak and narrower bandwidth (Δf).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual MCQs asking how altering R, L, or C affects the sharpness of tuning.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Impedance vs Frequency Resonance Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting total circuit impedance Z on the y-axis against frequency f on the x-axis, showing a distinct minimum at f<sub>r</sub> equal to R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At resonance, impedance is purely resistive and attains its minimum value, causing current to reach its maximum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate understanding of impedance minima and phase angle changes in series resonance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Angle vs Frequency Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of phase angle φ between voltage and current against frequency f, transitioning from negative values (capacitive) below f<sub>r</sub> to zero at f<sub>r</sub>, and positive values (inductive) above f<sub>r</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the phase curve at resonance is directly related to the Q-factor of the circuit.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in matching-type or assertion-reason questions concerning circuit behavior off-resonance.

solved_numericals.question: A series L-C-R circuit has an inductance L = 2 H, capacitance C = 32 μF, and resistance R = 10 Ω. Calculate the Q-factor of the circuit at resonance.
solution_steps: Identify the given parameters: L = 2 H, C = 32 × 10<sup>-6</sup> F, R = 10 Ω.
Use the formula for Q-factor: Q = (1 / R) × &sqrt;(L / C).
Simplify the term inside the square root: 2 / (32 × 10<sup>-6</sup>) = 1 / (16 × 10<sup>-6</sup>) = 62500.

solved_numericals.question: A series resonant circuit has a resonant frequency of 100 kHz and a bandwidth of 2 kHz. If the inductance is 0.5 mH, find the resistance R and the capacitance C of the circuit.
solution_steps: Identify the given values: f<sub>r</sub> = 100 kHz = 10<sup>5</sup> Hz, Δf = 2 kHz = 2 × 10<sup>3</sup> Hz, L = 0.5 mH = 0.5 × 10<sup>-3</sup> H.
Calculate the Q-factor using Q = f<sub>r</sub> / Δf = 10<sup>5</sup> / (2 × 10<sup>3</sup>) = 50.
Use the bandwidth formula Δω = R / L, where Δω = 2π Δf. Thus, R = (2π Δf) L.
Use the Q-factor formula Q = ω<sub>r</sub>L / R to find ω<sub>r</sub> = 2πf<sub>r</sub> = 2 × 3.1416 × 10<sup>5</sup> = 6.283 × 10<sup>5</sup> rad/s.
Alternatively, use resonant frequency formula ω<sub>r</sub> = 1 / &sqrt;LC to find C: C = 1 / (ω<sub>r</sub><sup>2</sup> L).

solved_numericals.question: In a series L-C-R circuit with L = 0.1 H, C = 10 μF, and R = 20 Ω, an alternating source of 20 V (rms) is applied at the resonant frequency. Find the voltage across the capacitor at resonance.
solution_steps: Calculate the resonant angular frequency: ω<sub>r</sub> = 1 / &sqrt;LC = 1 / &sqrt;(0.1 × 10 × 10<sup>-6</sup>) = 1 / &sqrt;10<sup>-6</sup> = 10<sup>3</sup> rad/s.
Calculate the Q-factor of the circuit: Q = ω<sub>r</sub>L / R = (10<sup>3</sup> × 0.1) / 20 = 100 / 20 = 5.
At resonance, the voltage across the capacitor is magnified by the Q-factor: V<sub>C</sub> = Q × V<sub>source</sub>.
Substitute the values: V<sub>C</sub> = 5 × 20 V = 100 V.

assumptions_and_limitations: The formulas assume a linear, time-invariant lumped-parameter R-L-C circuit.
The approximation Q = ω<sub>r</sub> / Δω is highly accurate for Q > 5 (narrowband condition).
Stray capacitances and inductances of connecting wires are neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A higher Q-factor means lower voltage across reactive components at resonance.
common_misconceptions.correct: A higher Q-factor means higher voltage magnification across the inductor and capacitor at resonance.
common_misconceptions.why: Q represents the amplification factor V<sub>L</sub> / V<sub>source</sub> = ω<sub>r</sub>L / R; thus, larger Q gives larger reactive voltages.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Q-factor has units of frequency or ohms.
common_misconceptions.correct: Q-factor is a completely dimensionless quantity.
common_misconceptions.why: It is a ratio of energies or reactances to resistance, making all units cancel out.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Increasing resistance R increases the Q-factor of a series LCR circuit.
common_misconceptions.correct: Increasing resistance R decreases the Q-factor and broadens the resonance curve.
common_misconceptions.why: R is in the denominator of the Q formula (Q = ω<sub>r</sub>L / R), so damping increases energy loss and reduces Q.

quick_revision: Q-factor is the ratio of resonant frequency to bandwidth: Q = ω<sub>r</sub> / Δω.
In series L-C-R, Q = ω<sub>r</sub>L / R = (1 / R)&sqrt;(L / C).
Q-factor measures voltage magnification across L or C at resonance: V<sub>C</sub> = Q V.
Higher Q-factor implies sharper tuning and lower energy dissipation per radian.
